notes: A PoiTouch in Sedgemire's place builders; tells.

look.speaker: The saying stone
look.text: A flat stone at the foot of the stair, worn hollow in two places the size of feet. Everybody who has stood here stood the same way, facing the ladder with their back to the carr, and said one name, once, plain. Over your head the cords under the deck turn a little in no wind. The hut is shut. It is not the dark of the moon.

say.speaker: The saying stone
say.text: You say it. It goes out over the carr flat and small, the way a name does with nobody to hear it, and nothing comes back. Nobody is here to take it. — But one of the cords under the deck, a green one, stops turning, and hangs quite still until you step off the stone.

speaker_name: The face on the fourth course
notes: A PoiTouch in Sedgemire's place builders; tells.

look.speaker: The face on the fourth course
look.text: Cut into the fourth course on the seaward side, a hand above the black water: a brow, two eyes, a long nose and a mouth set straight. The water has worn it soft, but not much. The reedfolk children dive from the top of the tower to touch it, and say it is good luck, and say it with the voice children use for things that are not luck at all. It is not a Builder's face. Anybody who has stood in the Choir's ash and looked up has seen it before: it is the face of the Thirteenth colossus, looking out to sea at something that is not there any more.

choices.text: Leave the face to the water.

notes: A PoiTouch in Sedgemire's place builders; tells.

look.speaker: The bell-rope
look.text: The rope runs down from the bell to the ringer's porch and is tied off on a cleat, worn shiny where his hands went. The quarter-glass on the sill has run out and nobody has turned it. The hut behind is cold and its door stands open.

ring.speaker: The bell-rope
ring.text: You haul on the rope and the bell speaks over the channel, once, and the reeds take it and carry it a long way. A while later, from up the channel toward Moreva, a boat's horn answers: somebody out there in the fog knows where the channel is now. — Then, from the other way, from under the water off the end of the landing, something knocks twice on the stage's posts, slow, the way you knock on a door you expect to be opened.

notes: A PoiTouch in Sedgemire's place builders; tells.

look.speaker: The high stew
look.text: The sixth stew is walled a man's height where the others are knee-high, and its sluice-board is down and wedged. There is no water in it. The mud at the bottom is dry and cracked and printed all over with the marks of something that lay in it a long while and turned and turned, and on the outside of the wall the stone is wet, in a broad dark band from the top down to the drag-marks, as if something very large and very slow had gone over it, and kept going, toward the channel.

notes: A PoiTouch in Sedgemire's place builders; tells.

look.speaker: Under the water
look.text: Through the black water, an arm's length down, the doorway of a reed house, the door open, and in it a lantern on its hook, lit. The flame does not move. Further in, past it, the shapes of a table and a bench and a pot on the hearth, all of it standing as it stood the night the water came. Every house in Mor'oul is the same. Nobody has ever found a record of a flood, and nobody in the Delta will light a lantern from one of these.

notes: A PoiTouch in Sedgemire's place builders; tells.

look.speaker: The lanterns of Saoul
look.text: Twelve stilts, a lantern lit on every one, oil in every one, though nobody in Saeva will say they pole down to fill them. You count them round the pool, and then again to be sure, and get thirteen the second time: the thirteenth is under the water in the middle of the pool, a little below the surface, quite steady, where no stilt is.

notes: A PoiTouch in Sedgemire's place builders; tells.

look.speaker: The knot-rail
look.text: Cords on the watch-rail, knotted close, a knot for every night the grey has come down over the scarp's lip. Thirty-one. They are tied in the boatwright's splice of the Nauves, very neat, and the last few are tied tighter than the rest, as if the hands that tied them were afraid they would come undone.

notes: A PoiTouch in Sedgemire's place builders; tells.

look.speaker: The Drowned Arch
look.text: The arch stands with the mere on one side and the reeds on the other and nothing either side of it: no wall, no road, no reason. The reedfolk say it was a door and the marsh was a room. Eel-boats pass under it from the mere side for luck, every boat, every time, and never once the other way. Somebody's luck-knot hangs from the keystone at the height of a boatman's hand.

choices.text: Walk through it from the landward side.
Go round it, the way everybody does.

through.speaker: The Drowned Arch
through.text: You step through. Nothing happens. — The reeds on the far side are the same reeds, the mere the same mere. Only, when you look down, your shadow is lying a little behind you, as if it had stopped to think about it and was only now catching up; and the luck-knot on the keystone, which you are sure was tied when you passed under it, is untied.

notes: A PoiTouch in Sedgemire's place builders; tells.

look.speaker: The knuckle-bone
look.text: A giant's knuckle, three bones of one finger-joint laid together on the top of the cairn, grey-white, pitted, each the size of a sheep. The Oskel clan set them pointing back up the dale, toward home: past this, the clans say, is not their memory's business. Somebody has turned them. They point into the fen now, and in clan sign that means follow, and under them in the cairn's top stones somebody has pushed a red wool cord in the Oskel knot, the knot a clan ties for a person, not a herd.

choices.text: Leave the bones where they point.

notes: A PoiTouch in Sedgemire's place builders; tells.

look.speaker: The Round Stones
look.text: Three stones on three islets, and between them the black water, wide enough that a voice has to carry to reach the next. The round goes from stone to stone: one choir begins, the next comes in as the first reaches the third line, the third as the second does. It does not end; somebody stops, and then somebody else. There is nobody on the islets now. The mats are wet.

choices.text: Sing the second voice, a little flat on the fourth line.

sing.speaker: The Round Stones
sing.text: You sing it, badly, the way you can, and on the fourth line your voice goes flat the way the hook said. The water takes it over to the far islet. — And there, on the far islet, where there was nobody, an old woman is sitting on the wet mats with her hands in her lap, weeping, and when you look again there is nobody.

notes: A PoiTouch in Sedgemire's place builders; tells.

look.speaker: The survey-cairn
look.text: A surveyor's pole on a cairn, a rag on it gone pink with weather. Sighted along it, the three stones make a dead straight line: the first on the flats, the second in the shallows, the third out in the water up to its shoulders, and the line runs on past it, out to sea, toward where the Salt Isles are said to be. The old quay's facing stones run across the line at the second stone. That was the shore. The chart in the Spire puts the shore here still.

notes: A PoiTouch in Sedgemire's place builders; tells.

look.speaker: The milestone
look.text: A milestone of the Builders' black stone standing in the shallows past the end of the road, the water round its foot, cut on its landward face with a number in the Builders' figures. It is not a distance from anywhere in Wickmere. Read the other way, as the reedfolk say the Builders read, it is a distance to somewhere, and the somewhere is out to sea. The figures are filled with something pale that catches the light under the water.

choices.text: Leave the stone to the sea.

notes: A PoiTouch in Sedgemire's place builders; tells.

look.speaker: The ore-cart
look.text: An Oskel ore-cart run off the end of the ford's causeway into the fen, one wheel sunk to the axle. The silver ore is still in it, a dozen lumps of grey galena with the bright shot in them, nobody's taken a piece. The carters' boots stand in the mud beside it, side by side, laced, as if two men had stepped out of them carefully and walked on into the fen barefoot. The tracks go a little way and then stop.

notes: A PoiTouch in Sedgemire's place builders; tells.

look.speaker: The figurehead
look.text: Under the bowsprit, a gull carved in pale wood with its wings swept back along the bows, and where a gull's head would be, a woman's: round-faced, a little heavy at the chin, her hair carved as a hood, her mouth open as if she had been about to call out to somebody on the shore. The salt has taken the paint off everything but the eyes, which are reedfolk indigo. The Moreva people who came to see her went home quiet: it is Senne Oul who keeps the dye-vats, to the life, and Senne Oul has never been further west than Oulea.

choices.text: Leave her looking up the carr.

notes: A PoiTouch in Sedgemire's place builders; tells.

look.speaker: The rags on the shrouds
look.text: Strips of indigo cloth tied along the shrouds, the way the reedfolk tie them on a boat that is not coming home. Every one of them has been untied and tied again, and not in any knot of the Delta: a double loop pulled flat, which is the Lakefolk's, from the other side of the downs. The knots are fresh. The mud round the hull has no footprints in it but your own.

speaker_name: The fire laid by the door
notes: A PoiTouch in Sedgemire's place builders; tells.

look.speaker: The fire laid by the door
look.text: A ring of stones at the crannog's door and the sticks stood in it in a cone, dry, ready, a twist of birch-bark tucked under for the light. Nobody has lit it. It was laid by somebody who knew the next one would come cold and wet, and laid well; and the ash under it is from last night's, swept, and the night's before, and the night's before that.

choices.text: Leave the fire for the next one.

notes: A PoiTouch in Sedgemire's place builders; tells.

look.speaker: The stakes
look.text: Every stake on the beds stands a row nearer the sea than it did: you can see the old holes in the mud behind each one, a row back, still wet. Each family's knot is on its own stakes, indigo for the Sas, rush for the Ouls, red for the Moreva cousins, and not one of them is out of its row; whoever moved them moved them all, together, the same way, in one tide, and did not tread the beds doing it. The reedfolk have stopped quarrelling over it. That is how you know they are frightened.

notes: A PoiTouch in Sedgemire's place builders; tells.

look.speaker: The footprints in the salt
look.text: The pan dried to a crust in one night, which a pan does not do; and across the crust, from the sea side, a line of bare footprints, a woman's or a child's, pressed clean through the salt to the clay. They go straight across, not hurrying, and stop at the landward bank. There are none going back, and none on the bank, and none in the next pan. The rakers have left this pan to dry and will not rake it.

notes: A PoiTouch in Sedgemire's place builders; tells.

look.speaker: The pale trough
look.text: The liquor in the other troughs is so dark you cannot see the cloth in it. In this one, the row nearest the Nave, it has gone the colour of a bruise healing, and the cloth lying in it is the blue of a sky in the Vale, and getting paler while you watch. The dyers say the fog. Loa Oul, who has steeped cloth here fifty years, says the drowned have been drinking it, and points at the trough's lip, where the reed is wet from the outside.

notes: A PoiTouch in Sedgemire's place builders; tells.

look.speaker: The prints on the planks
look.text: Bare feet, a grown man's and smaller ones beside them, printed dark and wet on the planks of the boardwalk, coming in out of the delta toward the gate. They are wet still, at noon, in the sun, and the planks round them are dry. They come as far as the gate and stop under the lintel, where the lanterns hang, side by side, the way people stop to be let in.

speaker_name: The lanterns on the last post
notes: A PoiTouch in Sedgemire's place builders; tells.

look.speaker: The lanterns on the last post
look.text: Sixteen lanterns hung from the last post's arms, each with a name painted round its paper in whatever hand the maker had: reedfolk names, a Lakefolk one, a dozen of the plain Vale names that Hester Wrenn paints, CARTER and DROVER where nobody knew more. They are lit for the drowned who came up with no name and nobody, and the reedfolk sing them the third voice of the round. One lantern, the newest, is pegged in the Mor weave and has no name on it yet.

notes: A PoiTouch in Sedgemire's place builders; tells.

look.speaker: The deckhouse
look.text: The master's deckhouse, its door swung open on one hinge. Inside, a bunk with the blanket folded, a bowl on the table with the spoon in it, a sea-chest with its lid up and nothing in it but a smell of cloves. The reeds have come up through the floorboards and stand round the table like people waiting to be served. On the wall over the bunk somebody has scratched a line of tally-marks, the Salt Isles way, in fives, and stopped at three hundred and nine, which the reedfolk say is how many days it is from the sea to here on foot, if you walk the way the water does.
